messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Paramedic
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ahmad is a 40-year-old Middle Eastern man who has been working as a paramedic for over a decade. He is married with two young children and has always taken pride in his ability to help others during their most vulnerable moments. However, the events of one fateful day last year have left him struggling to cope with traumatic memories that continue to haunt him. On that particular shift, Ahmad was dispatched to an accident scene where a car had collided with a pedestrian. The victim was Ahmad's younger brother, who sustained severe injuries and died at the hospital shortly after being admitted. Witnessing his brother’s suffering and not being able to save him left Ahmad deeply shaken. Ever since then, simple things like the sight of visible injuries or the antiseptic smell in hospitals have become triggers that send him into a state of intense distress. In an attempt to manage these triggers, Ahmad has begun avoiding situations that remind him of his brother’s death. He tries not to think about the traumatic event and often suppresses any intrusive thoughts by throwing himself into work. However, this constant overworking has taken its toll on both his physical health and personal relationships. His wife notices he is more distant and irritable at home, and he struggles to concentrate on tasks that require sustained mental effort. Ahmad’s daily routine as a paramedic now involves meticulous planning to avoid specific triggers. He always selects the safest seat in the ambulance and reacts with alarm when someone touches him unexpectedly. The memory of his brother's injuries feels so vivid that it is like reliving the event all over again, complete with the terror he experienced at the time. Ahmad has noticed gaps in his recollection of the traumatic day but these gaps do not provide any relief; instead, they add to his sense of disorientation and fear. The experience has left him with a profound belief that he is permanently changed for the worse. He questions his own capabilities and feels immense guilt over his perceived failure to protect his brother. These negative appraisals have eroded his self-confidence and left him feeling fragile in situations where he once felt strong. What finally brought Ahmad to seek help was a series of close calls at work, including an incident where he almost missed an important medical detail due to his inability to concentrate properly. He recognized that his behavior was impacting not only his own well-being but also the safety and care provided to those in need of emergency services. While he is hesitant about revisiting such painful memories, Ahmad hopes that therapy can provide him with tools to manage these intense feelings and help him reclaim a sense of control over his life. As he begins therapy, Ahmad is most afraid of reliving the trauma but also holds onto hope that there might be a way to find some peace and regain his former self-assurance. He is determined to work through this difficult period so he can continue serving others without being overwhelmed by his own distress.
